utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler. Welcome back --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- for another day of hearing. You know the affirmation to tell the truth still applies today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir is continuing his examination. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wish peace to this house and for all those present. And may God's will be done in these proceedings and may the outcome be as God wishes and not as I wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish welcome also to Mr. Butler. We are glad to have him here. Yesterday, Mr. Butler, we talked about the abuses and eventually the smuggling in connection with the convoys which were perpetrated by the army in Srebrenica. Please, have you reviewed any document that deals with these issues and the issue of the distribution of humanitarian aid? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents that I've reviewed in that respect, many of them which were discussed during my direct examination, some of them we've seen on cross-examination, reflect the view that the Bosnian Serb military and the Republika Srpska government had that UNPROFOR and other United Nations agencies, either wittingly or unwittingly, were providing supplies and military materials to the 28th Division and other Bosnian Muslim units within the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. It was a perception that the United Nations people were aware of. There had been a number of cases in the past where those issues had been flagged to their attention. I believe there are at least one or two cases where UN forces in and around Sarajevo were actually -- convoys were actually stopped that had war materials in them that should not have been there. So it was a continuing theme within that respect. Now, within the enclaves, as I've testified yesterday, certainly the Republika Srpska and the Army of the Republika Srpska were aware that once those convoys went into the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves, they would be powerless to control who the supplies went to. I mean, obviously the overwhelming predominance of the supplies were civilian materials for the civilian populations, but there was black marketeering, there was clearly diversion to the military forces of some of those supplies, and this was well known by all the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Now, please, concerning the supplies that were being sent to the army, something that you could read about even after the departure of UNPROFOR and the liberation of Srebrenica and Zepa and the exit of the BH Army and the civilian population from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specific to the issue of supplies to the army, and, again, as I've testified, most of the military supplies that were going to the 28th Division were either brought in or smuggled overland by soldiers of the 2nd Corps going over known smuggling routes, or in some cases that they were brought in surreptitiously via helicopter flights into the enclave. So again, in that respect, as I've noted, the goods that the military could appropriate from the civilian population, food stuffs, cooking oils, things of that nature, they did not bring in themselves. They used the auspices of the UN, essentially, to let the UN handle those civilian supplies and then appropriate them as they needed. But the strictly military technical equipment they had to bring in themselves over known routes - it was a relatively active smuggling regime that was going on over these routes - to allow the 28th Division to slowly bring in ammunition, weapons, things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us who gave them permission to bring that in, or did they do it illegally without anyone checking on them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "that," I'm not exactly clear what you're talking about. Are you referring to who gave permission for the civilian aid or who authorised the transshipment of military supplies?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I meant military supplies, because you said that -- it seems that you said that it was permitted, even though it was not permitted.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The United Nations going into Srebrenica, to my knowledge, never wittingly, or to their knowledge, took military supplies in that were going to be used by the 28th Division in the Srebrenica enclave. Now, the 28th Division itself undertook a programme with their headquarters in 2nd Corps in order to smuggle military supplies from the larger Bosnian Muslim territory held by 2 Corps behind the Bosnian Serb military lines in order to get it into the hands of the soldiers in Srebrenica and Zepa. Is that what you're referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Please, have you ever seen any report issued by a senior officer, commanders of UNPROFOR, relating to the illegal bringing in of weapons into Srebrenica, whether it was done illegally or through smuggling channels? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that particularly during the months of January, February, March of 1995 that many members of the United Nations forces in Eastern Bosnia were picking up on bits of information that had to do with outside military supplies coming into Bosnia, primarily through the Tuzla airport. Many of those supplies going to the 2nd Corps, some of those supplies subsequently making their way to the 28th Division in Srebrenica, and that the United Nations was reporting these outside supply -- military supplies coming in, which they viewed as a violation of the United Nations arm embargo. So if that's the context that you're referring to, I have seen those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you perhaps ever seen a report on the conversation done by Mr. Franken on the 31st of March, 1999? We are going to show you in order to facility your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for that purpose we need an exhibit, 1D207.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have on the screen the English and the Dutch version of this document. Is there a B/C/S translation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that we do not have a B/C/S translation, but I have a hard copy with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell me, have you ever seen this report that you are now reading that's an interview with Mr. Franken who had been a deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the OTP has interviewed Major Franken on a number of occasions. However, I am not sure that I've -- this doesn't look like an OTP originated product. I assume from the Dutch copy that I saw that this may be an interview that he did pursuant to the Dutch parliament's own investigation into Srebrenica. So I don't believe I've ever seen this particular document before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you help us: Who interview Mr. Franken? We can't see that from the text on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. Since the witness hasn't seen item number 1, let's see what it says there. But before that it says that the tape recording failed; the text below is a reconstruction of what was discussed. And then it says, under number one: "The ABiH army smuggled two combat armoured vehicles into the enclave via Sarajevo. This was notified by a Dutch OP. They were never found. Later it became clear that the Ukrainians in Zepa were missing a total of five. Bought or stolen by ABiH?" And then under 2 it says -- no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue, please explain what kind of document we have on the screen. Who did this interview with Mr. Franken?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This interview was done by NIOD, the institute for investigations, and a copy of that interview was provided to the OTP alongside other documents. If you permit me, I would like to read item number 1 -- or, actually, I have already read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The NIOD, the institution of investigations, is a Dutch institution investigating the events in Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. That's correct. It's their institute for war documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on with your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, after having read item 1, tell me, did you know anything about the fact that even heavy weaponry such as combat armoured vehicles were smuggled into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware that heavy combat vehicles such as BTR armoured personnel carriers were smuggled into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you trust this report by Mr. Franken?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a question of whether I trust it or not, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: As we have heard from you, Mr. Tolimir, it's not a report. It's a reconstruction of an interview of NIOD with Witness Franken. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That's all I wanted to point out for the record. But also, NIOD is a historical documentation centre; it's not really an investigative body. But it doesn't really matter, just as long as that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have seen some other documents in this trial from NIOD, so we are quite familiar with this institution. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. When Mr. Franken testified here, we asked him, on page 39, 3459, lines 15 to 19, and in the course of his testimony he said that he himself had seen armoured vehicles, two of them, passing through Srebrenica. And after that the Ukrainian unit from Zepa, in its logistical report, says - and this is information we received from the UN - reported the disappearance of five APCs. And then on page 3459, lines 24 and 25, and 3401, he replied that these were vehicles that had never been retrieved or found and that that was true. Now, please, were other members of the UNPROFOR, whose statements you've read, were aware of the fact that the BH Army was acquiring heavy weaponry, APCs, and other pieces of equipment in an illegal way by means of smuggling?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, what I can tell you is that I'm not aware of this issue. Having -- you know, as someone who has gone over, through the years, the documents of the Army of the Republika Srpska related to Srebrenica, I'm not aware of any report where the military units talk about the fact that they have captured two BTR armoured personnel carriers from the ABiH pursuant to the fall of the enclave. So if that fact happened, and those BTRs were ultimately taken over by the Army of the Republika Srpska after they were captured, it was never reported in their -- to their chain of command. I would also note the fact that with respect to the Ukrainian United Nations detachment in Zepa, I would find that fact rather difficult to believe in light of the very close known association between the local VRS forces at Zepa and the Ukrainian Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. We've reviewed what the general said, the cites regarding his statement that Franken testified that he himself saw armoured personnel carriers go through Srebrenica, and it -- we don't see that. So if the general could actually read the section he's referring to. There is a reference that Franken sees, in a report, that things were missing from Zepa, but we can't see what he's talking about, and I don't recall him saying he saw, you know, stolen personnel carriers going through Srebrenica. I mean, that -- perhaps I've forgotten that, but that sounds very strange to me. So if he can read what he's talking about, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will help everyone with the reference. That's the transcript of the 1st of July. It wasn't Mr. Franken who said that he saw it himself, but it's, rather, on page 3461, lines 8 to 9, said: [In English] "My OP only saw them entering the enclave at the south border. That is just a remark for the question before."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, we didn't receive a full interpretation of what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you can -- the best way is to have the relevant part on the screen and then we can check it. Page 3461, lines 8 to 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if we could start it at 7. You can see that that's a good place to start this. Line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. McCloskey is right. That's what I said, that Mr. Franken didn't say that he saw it himself but that that could be seen from the observation point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you see it on the screen. I will read the text into the transcript. Mr. Franken's answer is the following, I quote: "First, you concluded that I saw those vehicles in Srebrenica, which is incorrect. My OP," which means the observation post, "only saw them entering the enclave at the south border. That is just a remark for the question before." I would like to invite you, Mr. Tolimir, to -- if you quote something from the transcript or a statement, you should be very correct if you put that part to the witness. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is precisely my problem: That I never received the transcript in my own language and I have to rely on my notes which need not be fully precise because of the speed. So that's probably the reason why I wasn't precise. My apologies to you and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have a team. You have Mr. Gajic and other team members and you have assistance for interpretation and translation. So that this is a question of a good preparation of your cross-examination. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't want to go into the reasons why I have difficulties and why I do not use all the facilities that I should.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like to put the following question to Mr. Butler: What you have just heard, does it confirm or change the position that you've just expressed about the APCs? Thank you. The APCs, that is, which were smuggled into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it does not. Simply put: Again, my knowledge of this situation is based off of the military documents that I've read that cover the periods, obviously, before and after the fall of the enclave, primarily from the perspective of the Army of the Republika Srpska. I'm not aware of any military documents that reflect that units of the VRS took custody of these two vehicles or that they were captured by them after the fall of the enclave. I don't -- I hold open the possibility, obviously, that it occurred as Major Franken said, that his OP had reported this. But that fact and that fact that those vehicles had been captured by the VRS subsequent has never been reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I never said that the VRS seized the vehicles or captured them, and that's not the point. The point is, how were the vehicles smuggled into Srebrenica to begin with? How were they smuggled past the observation posts that observed them, and how this was not stopped? Let's now look at item 6 of the interview with Franken, the interview conducted by NIOD in 1999. He says, and I am quoting: "Weapons were regularly smuggled from Zepa straight through the Serbian lines, and local BSA commanders were richly rewarded for this. Occasionally, a BH army smuggling team ran into an ambush and several Muslim fighters were shot. But after this, the smuggling carried on as normal. Horses were sometimes used for this." And I will read item 7, which states: "Weapons were also regularly brought into the enclave from Tuzla." Was the VRS, therefore, rightly concerned about this and should not the VRS have taken all possible measures to make sure that no weapons, ammunition, nor equipment arrived or reached the enclave, i.e., a demilitarised zone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that not only was the VRS aware of the fact that weapons were being smuggled into Srebrenica, but that they were -- it was proper for them to be concerned and take the necessary measures to prevent these weapons from being smuggled in. I -- going back to point 6 on this, Major Franken's contention that local VRS commanders were complicit in this somehow, I'm not sure that I'm aware of that fact, at least from the VRS documents. I suspect that the intelligence and security branches of the VRS would have been very involved in that particular process, had they gained any awareness that local Bosnian Serb military commanders were somehow facilitating, for profit purposes, the supplies of weapons, ammunitions, into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. When reviewing the document 65 ter 05170, you spoke of the various restrictions imposed on UNPROFOR convoys that wanted to bring in supplies. Tell us, was the population in any way affected, adversely, by the restrictions that the VRS may have applied in respect of UNPROFOR convoys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: While it's difficult to quantify, I believe that there was some impact with respect to the restrictions on the UNPROFOR convoys, particularly related to medical care and certain other food stuffs. It's well documented by the Dutch Battalion that - as well as their own logistics - they would often provide excess medical or food stuffs supplies to the population, particularly segments of that population that were sick or that needed extra care. So in effect by restricting the supplies going into the UNPROFOR forces as part of the VRS campaign, it had, whether by design or not, it had an impact on the civilian populations in the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you aware of a case involving a fatality among the civilian population because of the shortage of medical supplies that the VRS may have prevented from entering into the enclave on an UNPROFOR convoy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak beyond generalities on this issue only because the actual day-to-day activities of the Dutch Battalion in the enclave, how they related to the civilian population, was not a focus of my analysis. I just didn't deal with that issue. My knowledge of that is based, in part, off of my own hearing of various members of the Dutch Battalion testify in certain situations here, so, again, I can't speak to that first-hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. In other words, you don't have a document that you may have reviewed and which could be referenced here for the Trial Chamber and which you would have used in expressing your basic view that this practice affected the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic document that I used in reference in my narrative with respect to the Dutch Battalion was the 1995 report that the Dutch themselves did after Srebrenica, as well as the United Nations report which also discusses aspects of the Dutch activities in the enclaves. That's the basis of my particular knowledge. I did not, because it wasn't necessary for what I was doing, I did not go through the daily activity reports of the Dutch Battalions -- or Battalion in Srebrenica to review what actions they did or did not take relevant to the civilian population there. And I was not part of the NIOD process as well, so I have no knowledge of what information they may or may not have come up with in that respect as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is my understanding correct, then: This was on the basis of what you heard and not based on documents that you could speak to as an expert? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is based on my understanding of those two reports. It is not based upon -- as well as what testimony I've heard, it is not based upon my own independent analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Tell me, did you find in these documents information about a medical organisation existing in Srebrenica which provided this sort of care for the population? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I believe the outside organisation you're referring to is the team from the medicine without frontiers organisation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't want you to guess what it is that I was thinking of. I just wanted to know what it is that you know.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. But I am aware that there was an independent medical organisation, the medicine without frontiers organisation, that did have a medical team inside of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Rather than looking at the document produced by this team, let's look at paragraph 26 of the document we have before us so that we could leave it once we are finished with it. There we have paragraph 26, and I quote: "The local situation for the population was, indeed, not great, but after the capture of the enclave, it turned out that there were huge food stocks there. The ABiH even dumped two lorries full of ammunition in the river." Paragraph 27: "The bombardments were, indeed, no small thing," and when I say -- I mean shooting and small arms fire, "but there was never any deliberate targeted shooting at DB III soldiers. Always right next to them. The ABiH did always try to get the DutchBat into a fight, and there were continuous attempts to maneuver the soldiers into a position in which the DutchBat would attract the fire of the Bosnian Serb army," et cetera. Based on the two paragraphs I've read, tell us, the statement made by Mr. Franken, to the effect that there were huge food stocks there, indicates that the situation in terms of food supplies was not disastrous in the enclave? Because he's talking about the situation as found after the population left the enclave.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is what Major Franken says. I mean, this is the report derived from an interview with them. I don't know that to be a fact one way or another. My analysis of the Srebrenica enclave did not include a total of food accounting that was captured in the enclave. My knowledge of it is based off of the VRS reports afterwards, and I'm not aware of VRS reporting that they are taking into custody these vast quantities of food. Whether they went into VRS custody, whether they went into civilian custody by the civilian commissioner of Srebrenica, I don't know. So I'm not in a position to comment one way or another on the issue of food and what was found after the fall of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One remark for the transcript. Page 14, line 25, through the next line, the words, I quote: "And when I say -- I mean shooting and small arms fire ..." These words are not part of the document but added by Mr. Tolimir. Just to have a clear record. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I did add this to clarify and I did not specify that I was doing that. I was just specifying what the word "pucanje," "shooting," means in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, do you know anything about the delivery of American weapons into the enclave? Did you come across such documents or do you have any sort of knowledge about it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no direct knowledge of it. I am aware, from reading the United Nations report related to Srebrenica, that there was United Nations reporting on flights go in Tuzla airport where arms were coming in. And certainly there was speculation that the United States had at least some role in those flights. But I don't know anything more than what is printed in the United Nations report related to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Let us now look at paragraph 41 of Franken's statement. Let's see what he has to say about it. He was the deputy commander of DutchBat in Srebrenica. I quote: "Franken is certain that there were American weapons deliveries to the ABiH army. These weapons were delivered in Tuzla and transported further from there." This is my question: Were UNPROFOR members also aware of the fact that there were American weapons come from Tuzla and from Tuzla to Srebrenica, as indicated by Mr. Franken in this report of his? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the knowledge of the UNPROFOR members, as evidenced by the United Nations report on that subject, a number of them were aware, and I believe one of the documents that you showed me yesterday that was authored by Mr. Akashi, in fact, noted also in that document that they were aware that there were weapon resupply flights coming into Tuzla. So clearly the UNPROFOR members had a contemporaneous knowledge of that event occurring. I am not aware based on my analysis of military documents, relating particularly from the VRS, that any US weaponry was captured there. Frankly speaking, it would be -- I would be surprised to find that that would be the case. Given that all of the combatants were fighting with weapons that were related to the former Warsaw Pact forces in the former Yugoslavia, putting weapon systems that cannot be adequately supplied in an isolated part of the battle-field doesn't make a lot of sense. It makes more sense that if the Americans were providing them weapons, they would be providing them weapons that they may have obtained from non-United States or non-NATO forces, because once you've provided them with these weapons, they could resupply themselves from captured ammunition stocks. So, again, I hold open the possibility, and it's well reported, that there were supply flights going into Tuzla, but I'm not aware of any American weapons being found in Srebrenica after the conflict -- or after, you know, captured by the VRS afterwards, and reported as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. You will see that even the Main Staff protested about this issue with the UN headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Tolimir please --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D196, yes, that's the number. Can we have D196.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you tendering the document 1D207?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, I would like it to be admitted with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D207 shall be assigned Exhibit D305. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We already have the next document on our screens. It's a document by the VRS Main Staff, dated the 24th of February, 1995, entitled: "Protest to the UNPROFOR Command in Zagreb, to General de Lapresle and to the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo, to General Smith in person. "At about 2010 hours on the 23rd of February, 1995, another transport plane landed on the auxiliary runway at Tuzla airport, loaded with weapons and military equipment and escorted by two NATO fighter aircraft, which protected it during its flight and while it was being unloaded. "Unfortunately, this has happened on a number of occasions recently, right in front of the eyes and the ears of NATO and UNPROFOR forces, in the air and at Tuzla airport itself, who are doing nothing to prevent the violation of the relevant Security Council resolution prohibiting imports of weapons and military equipment." This is my question: Mr. Butler, did you come across several documents and protests of the sort which cautioned about the fact that the resolution was being violated by NATO armed forces, the very same forces which provided security to the air-space above Bosnia-Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have seen United Nations documents which relate that, as we've discussed, that were happening at the time these violations were occurring, and I've read a number of witness interviews by United Nations observers who reported these same instances and discussed them. So I am very familiar with the events and allegations related to these particular violations of the cease-fire -- not cease-fire, but of the no-fly zone, as well as the arms embargo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Was the VRS then left with any other methods of control other than the methods of checks at check-points of the cargo that would possibly slip without proper notification? Was there any other method that they could have applied?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I believe that the VRS applied both the methods that were available to it, militarily speaking. The first one was the inspection regime that was in place to ensure that the United Nations was not overtly carrying armed materials into the enclaves, which they did. And the second one was the creation of military positions and ambushes along the known smuggling routes to try and interdict, to the degree that they could, the smuggling of weapons and arms into the enclave. And I would note that not only was it smuggling on the ground, but on a number of occasions the ABiH sought to smuggle in weapons via helicopter. And at least on one occasion that I'm aware of, the VRS was successful in shooting down a helicopter resupply flight. Now, with respect to the second avenue, the reality on the ground was that, just as I have discussed on a number of occasions, the VRS never had the adequate military manpower to completely seal off the enclave so weapons and supplies could not be smuggled in, but they were aware that the smuggling was occurring and that they were taking steps to combat it as much as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at D197.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the document we just saw on the screen, D196, was marked for identification pending translation. I was told that a translation is now available. Are you tendering the document now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, we are, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will now be Exhibit D196, and I would appreciate if, from time to time, the Defence could update us with the completion of translations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We now see D197. It's a document issued by the Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina, its military economic mission in Zagreb, which was sent to their office in Bihac, in the area of the 5th Corps of the BH Army, intended to -- personally for the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the letter they detail the items sent in the last dispatch, or shipment. The items mentioned are, without exception, mines and explosives. Is it possible for you to draw a conclusion as to how it was possible for these mines and explosives to reach the Bihac area, having travelled from Zagreb? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it's not. The conflict that occurred in the far western portion of Bosnia and Bihac is not an area that I've put any study into.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at this document, and just above the stamp you can see the last sentence. Now I hope you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, we need the next page in English, and we can retain the current page in the Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see, they just typed the license plate number of the truck that delivered this ordinance, UNHCR, and it was signed by Mr. Hajrudin Osmanagic, the military attache. Thank you. So can you see that this delivery came via the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no way of knowing whether that's true or not, whether it came under the auspices of the UNHCR or whether it was just a vehicle with UNHCR markings that was stolen or however it was done. I mean, I just don't know. I am not familiar with the area with respect to the military campaigns that were fought there, so I have no basis by which to offer an opinion as to how weapons were or were not being smuggled into the Bihac enclaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I note for the record that I only see a date in the stamp, which seems to be the 29th of May, 1993, although I'm not sure if that is really correct. Could the stamp please be enlarged. It is possible that the English translation is correct with the date of 29th of May, 1993, although the original is not very clear. It could be 1983, although at that time there was no embassy -- no BiH embassy in Croatia. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. But on the first page one can see, under the heading "-93," which indicates the year of 1993, which is the time of war. And during the war there was a military mission of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb, and also one can see in the stamp that the date is the 29th of May, 1993. I showed this document in order to demonstrate that it was the UNHCR who was also smuggling weapons and ammunitions in their vehicles, and Mr. Butler already commented on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at 1D198. In view of the fact that the time and the place is in dispute, whether this was during or before the war, in this document, again, we can see that it's clearly dated the 19th of May, 1993, and the sender is the Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... one correction for the transcript: The accused requested Exhibit D198.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, please wait for the end of the translation and then give us the number, Mr. Registrar. Once more, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The requested exhibit was D198. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you can see this exhibit which says that the 5th Corps of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, strictly confidential number 01/1-1690-2, 19th May, 1993, logistical report on receipt of shipment of ubs through UNHCR, and below it is listed what was carried by the UNHCR from Zagreb and delivered to the 5th Corps, including 50.000 rounds of ammunition; then 20.000 rounds of 7.62 millimetre; 12.000 of detonating caps; nitroglycerin gun powder, and so on and so forth. And finally Hexogen-explosive and rocket fuel. This was also shipped from Zagreb to Bihac. My question is: Was the UNHCR also used for the transportation and smuggling of weapons and ammunition for the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to clarify this document, the weapons that you list off are not those that were actually delivered. Those are subsequent to a future request. They're requesting those amounts of ammunition. However, if you go into the body of the first paragraph again, it does particularly note that through the particular channel that they are receiving these supplies, albeit through some mechanism of the UNHCR, they recognise that the maximum secrecy is necessary in order to protect the way that these supplies are being received. Again, whether large portions of the UNHCR are complicit in this or whether, you know, individual members of the UNHCR have been bribed or have been coopted to participate in this process is not clear from this document. But, I mean, so we're not in dispute. Certainly, the VRS by 1995 had more than adequate reason in their mind to believe that military supplies could be smuggled in via those routes. Which leads me back to my earlier conclusion that the VRS is justified -- or was justified at the time in instituting an inspections regime to make sure that the smuggling of military supplies in humanitarian goods was not happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. It's correct. One can see that from what was written by the 5th Corps commander to the embassy in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see D199. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see this document on our screens. It's another document issued by the Embassy of the Republic of BH in Croatia. And it speaks about the delivery of 70 tons of D-2 fuel. The haulier, as stated in the fourth row, is UNHCR, or the entity carrying out the transportation. My question is as follows -- or maybe first it would be better if you read the document and then I can pose a question. Or maybe I can read paragraph 3: "Should the UNHCR distribute the diesel to other institutions as humanitarian aid, since they do not know where the diesel comes from, these institutions must issue a specific quantity of diesel to the 5th Corps in accordance with the needs of the 5th Corps, and the rest must be reimbursed as agreed with the 5th Corps command. "The 5th Corps command shall send me a report on this matter." This was also signed by Osmanovic [as interpreted], and the date is -- I'm sorry, military attache Osmanagic, and it's dated the 13th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a correction: It was not signed by Mr. Osmanagic, but signed by another person for the military attache Osmanagic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for this correction. It is correct. It was signed by Ibrahim Hadzic, the representative of this office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can one deduce from this document that the UNHCR is supplying fuel by stating the civilians as recipient but in fact providing it to the army? Have you come across any similar documents when you studied the papers relating to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to your second question first: I have not, with respect to Srebrenica, come across any document which would reflect something this overt as was occurring in Bihac. I would also -- I'm not sure what to conclude from the particular document also, other than the fact that while I concur the UNHCR is part of the fuel distribution process, at least the second and third lines of that last paragraph reflect the fact that members of the UNHCR themselves don't know where the fuel is coming from and who the final originator is supposed to be, and it's actually holding open the possibility that they may inadvertently deliver parts of that fuel to humanitarian organisations since they don't know that it's destined for military aid. So, again, whether or not the entire UNHCR apparatus in Western Bosnia was complicit in this organisation or whether select members or parts of it were, obviously from these documents it lays out a situation where the ABiH and the government -- or through the embassy in Zagreb had created a pipeline to use a UN agency as a means of supplying aid to their forces in Bihac. Now, again, I agree with your -- you know, what I've said earlier on this. Certainly by 1995 the VRS would have had enough information about these various schemes that they had more than adequate grounds to institute an inspection regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. If there were no troops in Srebrenica and if there were no tanks that required this fuel, would you agree, then, that the VRS was capable of precisely estimating the quantity of fuel required by the population and to stop any surplus amounts that might be used by the army, because the VRS knew exactly what quantity of fuel was needed by the civilian population and what quantities were needed by a military unit, for example?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that based on the VRS's understanding of what the ABiH had in the enclave, that they certainly did believe that they had an ability to accurately calculate what fuel would be required going into the enclave. They should have had -- you know, setting aside the fact that the ABiH would have been trying to deceive the VRS as to their true strength, the VRS should have had an accurate picture of the materials that the UNPROFOR, as well as the various civilian agencies in the Srebrenica enclave, possessed, to include diesel/electric generators, things of that nature. Not necessarily vehicles, but obviously machinery that's important for the civilian population that runs on that type of fuel. So, yes, the VRS should have been able to accurately assess, based on the information that they had at the time, what the normal fuel accountability should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If the VRS had a criteria, for example, a battalion needed this and this quantity of fuel for their vehicles, was it possible for them to know the quantity needed by an UNPROFOR battalion and could they assume that some of the quantities were shipped elsewhere and stored elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VRS could and did assume a number of things related to that. The -- the VRS would have had an ability to seek to estimate the monthly fuel usage of the UNPROFOR and to calculate, in their mind, how much fuel would be needed. The UNPROFOR DutchBat, as far as I'm aware, provided their actual fuel usage to the UNPROFOR headquarters. They did not -- that information was not available to the VRS. So the first thing that you will have is a gap between the VRS calculations of fuel being used by the Dutch Battalion and the Dutch Battalion's actual fuel usage. The other factor that I suspect would play in there is that, particularly within the military, all military units, to include those in peacekeeping forces, would like to establish and maintain a reserve of fuel and other important technical items in the event of a supply disruption so they were not immediately impacted. While I suspect that the Dutch Battalion would liked to have created this reserve of fuel, it would not be uncalled for for the VRS to look at the creation of a fuel reserve by the Dutch as something that could be used by the ABiH potentially. So there is a lot of different ways that the VRS's calculations of the fuel that the Dutch would use or should be using versus the actual Dutch fuel consumption as well as their -- the Dutch requirements to put together a fuel reserve in case of disruption, and why the two parties would not be able to agree on how much fuel was actually being used versus what was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Do you know that or whether UNPROFOR of Srebrenica provided fuel for the buses that transported the civilian populations from Srebrenica to Tuzla in accordance with the agreement on the evacuation? Colonel Karremans from UNPROFOR himself proposed that UNPROFOR provide fuel for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to -- there is no facts in the record, and I think it was just a mistake, that the general knows that the -- the buses did not go from Srebrenica to Tuzla. They went, and I'm sure as he'll agree, to the Luka area right at the confrontation line, a good ways from Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. That's correct. The buses couldn't go to Tuzla, but they did reach the border of that area, where it was decided that they would be offloaded from the buses and that the population would proceed on foot across the separation line until they were received in the BH territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But I'm asking you, do you know if United Nations provided fuel for the buses to transport the populations into the Muslim territory from the territory of Republika Srpska in compliance with the signed agreement and that this instruction was issued personally by Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge is that they did not. From the review of documents that I have done related to the buses and truck transports, the fuel that was used in those vehicles primarily came from civilian commercial stocks that were at the Vihor Transportation Company in Bratunac. Now, the UN did send down a tanker with fuel and several days later it reached there, and what happened was that that fuel that in fact went to Vihor was used to restock that supply there. So potentially three or four days afterwards, the fuel was reimbursed. But the fuel that primarily filled up the buses and the trucks through the various days of the 12th and 13th originated from existing fuel supplies at the Vihor Transportation Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tolimir please repeat the name of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you please repeat the whole question, and especially the name of the battalion. The interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, do you know what happened with the reserves of fuel at the Dutch compound in Potocari; to whom was it distributed; or was it used to fill the tanks of the buses that were transporting the Muslim population from Srebrenica after the signing of the agreements?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I don't know what did or did not happen with respect to the fuel reserves of the Dutch Battalion. I do know that the Office of the Prosecutor is in possession of particularly detailed lists of civilian buses that were filled up at the Vihor commercial plant -- or commercial transportation company in Bratunac that were used as part of the movement of the civilians out of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if the general has evidence that there were fuel reserves of DutchBat, as he's built into that question, I think it would be appropriate for him to reference us to what he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I asked Mr. Butler if he knew what happened with the fuel reserves of the DutchBat and he gave the answer that he gave. It is up to me to put questions, not to provide proof and evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The objection would be that his question assumed a fact not in evidence. And that is a standard objection. And I don't generally go technical on that, but if he's going to assume something like that, he is -- it's incumbent upon him to either ask about that, was there reserves, or establish that there were reserves. Given the answer that Mr. Butler gave, it's not necessarily objectionable, but Mr. Butler said he was not aware of that, so that's why that's an appropriate objection, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your question was if Mr. Butler knew what happened with the fuel reserves of the DutchBat. It would be more appropriate to ask Mr. Butler if he knows anything about fuel reserves, and then the next question could be to ask if he knows anything about what happened to these reserves.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. My question was about the reserves. Since I did not get an answer, we are going to show a video-clip of the discussion between Mr. Mladic and Mr. Karremans, and in this video clip Mr. Karremans is offering to provide fuel. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We may do that, but after the break. We must have our first break now, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we were able to see that there were many possibilities for smuggling weapons, ammunition, fuel, et cetera. Let us now look into the rights of the party which let's these items pass through, the rights arriving from the Geneva convention.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D1004, this is the 4th Geneva Convention, relative to the protection of civilian persons in times of war. We are interested in Article 23 which is at page 8 in English and 5 in Serbian. My apologies, the other way around, page 8 in Serbian and 5 in English. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me read the article, Article 23: "Each High Contracting Party shall allow the free passage of all consignments of medical and hospital stores and objects necessary for religious worship intended only for civilians of another High Contracting Party, even if the latter is its adversary. It shall likewise permit the free passage of all consignments of essential food stuffs, clothing and tonics intended for children under 15, expectant mothers, and maternity cases. "The obligation of a High Contracting Party to allow the free passage of the consignments indicated in the proceeding paragraph is subject to the condition that this Party is satisfied that there are no serious reasons for fearing." Under a: "That the consignments may be diverted, used for different purposes, and not -- so that the consignments might be used for purposes other than the ones they intended for. "b. That the control may not be effective; or "c. That a definite advantage may accrue to the military efforts or economy of the enemy through the substitution of the above-mentioned consignments for goods which would otherwise be provided or produced by the enemy or through the release of such material, services, or facilities as would otherwise be required for the production of such goods. "The power which allows the passage of the consignments indicated in the first paragraph of this Article may make such permission conditional on the distribution to the persons benefitted, thereby being made under the local supervision of the Protecting Powers. "Such consignments shall be forwarded as rapidly as possible and the power which permits their free passage shall have the right to prescribe the technical arrangements under which such passage is allowed." My question: In view of the provisions of Article 23, the VRS, as a party which has allowed the humanitarian aid to transit the territory under its control on its way to Srebrenica, was it entitled to exercise full control, including the control of the distribution of the humanitarian aid, with a view to ensuring that it not be abused? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were, as specified here, and my understanding, again, is that the -- if one assumes that the United Nations functions as the protecting power in Bosnia and that the High Contracting Parties are, in fact, the warring parties, the Republika Srpska can and did use the offices of the protecting power to manage the distribution of those civilian supplies. So I believe that both, as a matter of law, in fact, what happened in Bosnia, with respect to the humanitarian supplies, happened in compliance with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now look at paragraph b of this particular article, "that the control may not be effective." This is one of the conditions based on which it may not be permitted. Are the conditions, a, "that the consignments may be used for different purposes, other purposes," and, c, "that the enemy may use them for military purposes." So please, if these three conditions were not met based on the indications arising from situations, did the VRS have the right to deny passage of humanitarian aid? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would note that I'm not an international law specialist, so I don't want to provide anything that gets couched as legal advice, but certainly within the confines of these articles the VRS - not necessarily the army but certainly at the political level, the government of the Republika Srpska - could have seen fit to terminate the arrangements by which the United Nations protection forces acted as a protecting power. Now, I suspect that you're going to have an interesting legal discussion with the rights, as specified in the Geneva Conventions, between High Contracting Parties to conduct conflict, versus the legal obligations of those same High Contracting Parties to follow the obligations and resolutions of the United Nations Security Council and how they're binding and under what circumstance, and that is something that is well above my head to comment on. So while I take your point as to what Article 23 says in its face, I would just remind you and the Court that there were other factors in play with respect to the United Nations and Security Council resolutions seeking to be implemented along the same lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. The VRS across which territory these convoys travelled, did it have reason to doubt that some of the aid would end up in the hands of the BH Army, given the fact that a military unit was stationed in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. As I've indicated from my review of the VRS documents, they believe that they had adequate information available to them that established the basis that some of the aid that was being given to civilians was being diverted for military purposes. I mean, the VRS was very clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday we saw documents indicating that some of the humanitarian aid was set aside for the military. We saw it yesterday in the report D80 drawn up by a municipality president. It was indicated that this was done on a monthly basis. This is my question: The percentage of aid which was set aside for the military, be it 20 or 30 per cent - let's leave that aside - could it have been withheld by the VRS given the fact that it was aware of this aid being shipped every month?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could Mr. Butler be allowed to see the document that this question appears to be based on? I mean, it -- the question appears, on its face, to be based on a document and then there are percentages that are actually mentioned, so I would ask that we be able to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let's have D80 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To answer your first assertion: I'm not sure that this document alone makes the case that humanitarian aid was set aside for the military. I -- it reflects the fact that the military is acquiring the supplies. Whether it's being set aside deliberately or whether it's been appropriated without the approval of civilian organs or because the civilian organs are powerless to stop it is an open question, but it is coming off civilian supplies. Answering your second question - and agreed, I have no way of knowing what the percentage could or is - could the VRS have been aware of these factors and have then sought to decrement the supplies coming in accordingly, I have no idea if the VRS could have been aware of this specific information and diversions. My reading of the VRS documents does not reflect that they had this specific level of awareness of the supplies being diverted. They had a general knowledge that they were being but certainly nothing to this level of specificity. Whether or not they could have consequently decremented that is, quite frankly, more a political decision than a military one. The -- politically, VRS could have made an argument that the supplies, if they could provide a percentage, should be decremented by that such to ensure that they did not follow into military hands, and, of course, I expect the United Nations humanitarian organisations would have significantly pushed back against that assertion, because of the impact that it would have had against the civilian population. I would also note that as a practical aspect it would have probably not been an effective measure for them to take, because, as both you and I are aware, in a military environment most often our needs come first, before the civilian population. Which means that in order to maintain the military capacities of fighting forces, it's not like the military would go without the military supplies that they felt that they needed. What would in fact happen is that they would continue to take those supplies from the civilian population and that it would, in fact, simply function to increase the hardships that the civilian population was operating under.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. This was a document you saw yesterday. Below the heading it says, To the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 5 June 1995. Now I will show you a different document, on the basis of which you will be able to make an accurate calculation of the percentage of aid set aside for the military.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look D213 in e-court. We can see the document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the Serbian version we can see that all the months were covered in terms of aid reaching the enclave. Captain Slavko Novakovic signed it. He was charged with humanitarian aid in the Drina Corps. The heading does state the Drina Corps command. This is a document which relates to 1994, and one can use it to conclude that the situation was more or less the same in 1993, because the size of the population did not vary much between the two years. I will show you another list for 1995 for the months for which calculations were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we move to another document, I would like to see the full heading of this document in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There, it says: "The Command of the Drina Corps," and there's nothing else there. The items missing from the English translation are numbers. They didn't copy them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I wanted to see the full headline. Now I see it, the description, what kind of list it is. And it's related to 1994. Thank you. Please go ahead. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just also see that the B/C/S goes up to 38, this goes to 25, so there must be more to this. If we could get at some idea of how much there is on this list. Does it go on and on, is there more text, or is it just a few more numbers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We see here the last item is number 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go ahead, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can provide the originals for the Trial Chamber to look at, and then you can get the clear picture of the document in the originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document is already in evidence and we have it on the screen. That is quite sufficient. I just wanted to see the full description of the document in English. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first list related to Zepa. Can we look at 1D704, which is the shipment of the humanitarian aid for the enclave of Srebrenica in 1994. Thank you. Yet again the translation includes only -- oh, there is no translation at all. Can we see both pages. The table relates to the entire year, medical supplies, medication, and it was signed by Captain Slavko Novakovic, who drafted the document and was charged with these issues within the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: Based on the two documents about the needs of the civilian population in Zepa and Srebrenica in 1994, could the VRS make an assessment of the required quantities of food stuffs and other necessities in the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it, from an abstract perspective, that any professional logistician - and certainly there were some on the VRS Main Staff -- or VRS Main Staff and Drina Corps Main Staff - could have made a general assessment as to how much general civilian and humanitarian supplies a set civilian population might have required under the circumstances. The -- there are obviously a lot of variables involved. Knowing the number of the civilian populations, having accurate figures with respect to the ages and medical requirements of various segments of that population are going to be important. I don't know that the VRS specifically had those numbers. But I suspect that you could make a ballpark, as we say in America, estimate as to what the supplies -- what a basic civilian population might need.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can these documents be admitted into evidence, please, and we will then present a different document relating to the same issues but from the perspective of the Muslim side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document D213 is already in evidence. For the second one, 1D704, we don't have an English translation; therefore, it will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D704 shall be assigned Exhibit D306 marked for identification pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we now look at D212 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us see how these humanitarian needs were viewed by the Muslim side. Thank you. We have the document now. It was sent to -- it was sent from Sarajevo on the 27 of February, 1995, to the Zepa municipality, the president of the municipality. And it reads: "Dear sir. "We have received a UNHCR report on humanitarian aid deliveries to Zepa for the period between the 1st of December, 1994, and the 15th of February, 1995. The report shows that on average 85 per cent of the aid was successfully delivered, which is satisfactory. This is the breakdown of the articles delivered". And we have quantities in tonnes. Listed are leguminous plants, meet, fish, cheese, rice/flour ... milk, oil, salt, sugar, and there are various columns listing various figures. And the last column reads percentage achieved. You can tell that in five cases, five articles, let's start from the bottom, salt, 120 per cent was the percentage achieved in -- against the needs expressed. Then we have rice/flour, meat, et cetera. Let's read through to the end of the document: "In the days ahead, a relatively good supply of sugar is expected since large quantities have arrived in Belgrade. "It can be concluded from the above data that the UNHCR is providing a relatively good supply of goods to Zepa, and we continuously monitor this and maintain permanent contact with them. "Yours faithfully. "Dr. Hasan Muratovic. "Minister." This is a minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is my question: Wasn't even the minister -- a minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina happy with the distribution of the humanitarian aid by the UNHCR in the course of -- sorry, not -- 1995 -- or, rather, from December to February 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this document reflects that from the period 1 December 1994 through 15 February 1995 that it is their view that the aid delivered was satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you, as an analyst find any documents testifying and confirming that the aid received by Zepa across the territory Republika Srpska was sufficient?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not review documents with respect to aid going into the Zepa enclave per se to determine whether or not the aid going into the Zepa enclave was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Was this being monitored by Minister Muratovic and did he express his satisfaction in this document by claiming that the deliveries supplied to Zepa are at a satisfactory level?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, as I've indicated in my prior answer, between the set period Dr. Muratovic was satisfied with the aid coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, can we look at another document in e-court, which is D209.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since this document covers the period from December 1994 until February 1995, let us look at the situation in March and April of 1995. It pertains to Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. We see here that this document was produced by the Drina Corps on the 3rd of May, 1995. This is a breakdown of humanitarian aid to the Muslims enclaves for March and April 1995. We have various columns. In the first one is the description of goods; the next one indicates the quantity in tonnes, and it relates to the months of March and April and the enclaves of Srebrenica, Gorazde, and Zepa. Now, please, if we look at the quantities. Let's take just one example of one of the staple items, such as flour or beans, which is under number 2. Did you ever analyse whether these quantities were enough to meet the needs of the Srebrenica, Gorazde, and Zepa enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. As I indicated before, I am not a professional logistician, and as a result I have no -- I do not have the professional background in order to make those kinds of -- the analysis, let alone judgements, behind them. So with respect to analysing whether these delivered amounts would be sufficient for whatever the population, I just have no basis to make those calls.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Could a logistics person be able to decide whether 32 tonnes of flour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 300 tonnes of flour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- would be enough to feed three -- 35.000 people?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to believe that there are people on UNHCR staff as well as other professional logistical organisations who can make those calculations. I assume there are, I just -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Have you ever found a document in which it says that the enclaves were suffering from shortages of flour and other staple foods as well as baby formulas, medical supplies, hygiene items, and things of that nature? Do you have any reference in that respect?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't. I did not review UNHCR documents related to supplies going into Srebrenica. The best people to ask that question to would obviously be those UN officials as well as the Dutch Battalion people who were there who were making their own independent observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Let me show you another document from 1994 sent to the Drina Corps. It relates to potentially contentious issues with regard to the distribution of UNHCR humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D852. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We have the document, but I've just been told that there is no English translation. I'm going to read it out. It is stated in the heading: "Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, confidential number 10/14-29, 16th January, 1994. "Assessment of the order of the president of the RS." Then there is a reference to this order. And then it goes on to say, I quote: "Pursuant to the order issued by Dr. Radovan Karadzic, president of RS, item 3, confidential number," this and this, "shall be amended to read as follows: 'All contentious issues that might arise with representatives of UNPROFOR and military observes shall exclusively be resolved through Corps commands and the Main Staff of the VRS. As for international humanitarian issues, these issues shall be resolved through the government co-ordinating body for humanitarian aid.' "Signed, Commander Lieutenant General Ratko Mladic." My question is: From this stamp can we see who the sender of this telegram is, and does this confirm that this is an authentic document dated the 16th of January?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart was able to find an English translation of this document, just so everyone knows that. I'm not sure how we can use it. One sec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is a Defence document. Perhaps it could be uploaded as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told by Mr. Registrar: If Ms. Stewart would send this translation to the Registrar, it could be uploaded and displayed on the screen together with the B/C/S original. There we have it on the screen thanks to the OTP. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am grateful to Mr. McCloskey and his team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, now you can see the English version of this document. Now, based on this document can one draw a conclusion that the president of Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic, and the commander of the Main Staff, Ratko Mladic, resolved all the issues through the organs responsible for monitoring and analysing the delivery of humanitarian aid to the enclaves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure, off of a solitary document, I can draw a conclusion. What this document appears to be is part of the ongoing process. This document - and at this point I don't have the English translation yet up on my screen - I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Court Usher will assist you to get it on the screen. Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What this document appears to be is a response to the president of Republika Srpska who has issued an order regulating these contacts and disputes, and this appears to be General Mladic is responding to that order, essentially making an amendment to that order back to the president with his recommendation of what the text should read in that particular item. Without having the base item to go behind and looking at it in its entire context, I can't answer your question whether I can conclude whether all of these issues are solved or regulated or whatever. I mean, this is just one fragmentary piece.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. I understood from your answer that it was Mladic who was amending something and sending it to Karadzic. Couldn't it be the other way around? I think that Mr. Karadzic is instructing Mr. Mladic how to solve the problems.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, without seeing the base document and understanding the genesis behind it, it's difficult to say exactly what this is. I'm only operating off of this one particular document. Again, what it appears to me to be is that there is -- has been published by the president of the Republika Srpska some definitive guidance on these issues in that base document, which is 01 [sic] 128/94 and that president -- or that General Mladic is looking for having at least one of those particular issues amended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you help me: This document, signed by Ratko Mladic, to whom was it sent? I can't see an addressee of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is sending this to all the units so as to inform them about the amended procedure for solving the dispute with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations, and he is passing on the solution as provided by President Karadzic. Although it's not stated, but when you have a document of this kind, that means that it's being sent to all the units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this assessment. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, have you found any document saying that the population was leaving the enclaves and that the humanitarian aid that was taken in early 1994 as a criterion for the needs to be met in the course of 1995, did it reach the population?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could that be broken down? I mean, "is there any document that they were leaving the enclave." I mean, there are so many documents about them leaving the enclave. I'm sure the general has something more specific in mind. But if he could be more specific, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
