utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. I will call up a document produced by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Which is D144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you tendering 1D852?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you for reminding me. We do tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Due to the help by the Prosecution, there is a translation. I hope that the parties and the Registry will be able to connect the translation with the original B/C/S document and then it will be received as a document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D852 shall be assigned Exhibit D307 marked for identification pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it the parties will communicate about the uploading of this document. It is not in e-court yet. It should be -- it is the duty of the Defence, in co-operation with the Prosecution. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a document that I asked for. Can you look at line 13 from the top, which begins with the words: "All the individuals complaining about the shortage of food and for that reason intend to leave these areas. We have found possibilities for providing assistance in this regard. However, in the summer months it is as if some unknown wave flows through the people, suddenly creating a euphoria, that the best solution is to leave for Tuzla. This literally causes waves throughout the entire area, and the majority of people are then ready to leave. Such has been the case in recent days. "Pursuant to the Order of the commander of the 28th Army Division ... dated 27th May, 1995, all movement by individuals or groups of people, particularly soldiers, between the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves is forbidden without prior written permission from the unit commander in the case of members of the armed forces, for which the consent of the division command is also required. Pursuant to the same Order, the commands of all units in the division zone of responsibility are obliged to make use of the intelligence and military security service organs to gather information on all persons intending to leave the safe area for other free territories ..." So in this first paragraph, where the order of the command is being referred to, does it say that people are complaining about the shortage of food and that that was the reason for their intention to leave the areas but that solution has been found to provide assistance? Did the command decide that that was not a sufficient reason for people to leave the area and that they have found a way of getting around this issue by increasing the reserves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says, sir, is that for all those who complain of a lack of food and for that reason intend to leave these areas, we have found possibilities for providing assistance in this regard. It does not specify, at least the part of the document that I can see, how they were going to deal with that issue and whether or not increasing food reserves are a part of that, assuming food reserves even existed. What it says is what it says. There's not enough to read into what they actually mean behind that particular line, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. But this was written by the 28th Division which is there together with the population; therefore, they are capable of finding a solution and offering assistance in that respect. Is that true or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with your assessment that they're there and they are in a position to offer a solution. What I'm just saying is that they don't specify in the lines that you've talked about -- there's no -- there is no details as to what those potential solutions are. It just says that possibilities -- you know, that we have found possibilities for providing assistance in this regard. I mean, I take your assumption that it could mean distributing more food, but it doesn't say that. So, I mean, that's my answer to your question. What it says is what it says. It does not specify what the measures are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Butler, please, could that problem have been solved in any other way other than by giving food to those who are complaining that there was the shortage of food?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect that from a military disciplinary point of view there were other ways that the issue could have been solved. For example, given the context of this document that people are leaving, in part, with their families or in extended groups, by putting more rigorous measures on the members of the military to keep track of them and potentially even put those in detention who they suspect may flee, that would cause those individuals and their families to remain in the enclave, because they would have no other means of getting out. So there are more harsh measures that could have been put into place beyond the simple aspect of increasing the food supply to certain individuals or groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, Mr. Butler. Maybe we were mistranslated when we quoted this, but this is a report from the 28th Division, saying that all those complaining about the food were taken care of. And the only way that they could have been taken care of was by giving them food. Can we please look at the first paragraph of this document, in view of the answer that you gave us. The document which was sent on the 19th of June, 1995, it was sent to the command of the 2nd Corps, and paragraph one states: "The problem of members of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and civilians leaving the Srebrenica and Zepa safe areas in the direction of Tuzla, Kladanj, and Serb has been present since the first days of demilitarisation of this area." In other words, this was a steady process that did not only take place in 1995. "During this entire period, the military and civilian authorities in Srebrenica have taken a number of measures to prevent such departures, yet all of these measures have not yielded significant practical results." And he goes on to say that this was due to a shortage of food but that they had been successful in providing food to all those who expressed a shortage of it. He goes on to say: However, in the summer months it seems that suddenly some unknown wave flows through the people, a craving of departures. So this is my question: Were there permanent departures of the civilian population from Srebrenica to Central Bosnia as is stated here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That question I can definitely answer. As you will note, and as this document notes, the issue of civilian population within the enclave, many of them wanting to leave, was an issue that began from the very beginning of the creation of the enclave. The enclave was, in fact, created in part because people who had been forced out of the Kamenica and Cerska areas by the Bosnian Serb military offensives in early 1993, January, February, March, and had been pushed into Srebrenica, were, in fact, in April of 1993 being put on trucks by the VRS and evacuated out of that town. That evacuation out of the town of Srebrenica in 1993 was stopped by the BiH government, which viewed that as --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- by allowing those people -- by allowing those people to depart, was making themselves complicit in an ethnic cleansing campaign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please switch off your microphone. Please switch off your microphone, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So to that degree it has been well established that a large percentage, and perhaps the majority of the people, who were actually in the Srebrenica enclave were not actually from Srebrenica. They were refugees who had been pushed out of their village and home areas and other parts of Eastern Bosnia. So there was always a desire on their part to leave the Srebrenica enclave. I mean, from a political perspective, there was always a desire by the ABiH government to not allow them to leave the enclave, because if that portion of the civilian population left the enclave, it would presumably directly impact any legitimacy to the argument that they had that those safe areas needed to be maintained. So I agree with General Tolimir's assertion that from the very beginning of the enclave, for a variety of reasons, civilians who were trapped in those enclaves wanted to get to Central Bosnia or out to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. We will be discussing this issue later in some of the questions, but let's complete this issue. Was the problem so comprehensive that even the division commander had to apply restrictive measures in 1995 to prevent the population from moving out of the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an ongoing problem. Much to the same degree that it was always an ongoing problem of manpower for the VRS. The family men -- the males of the families who were trapped in the Srebrenica enclave were, in fact, conscripted into the 28th Infantry Division. If they were to escape with their families, that would obviously have a corresponding negative impact on the material and the military ability of the 28th Infantry Division to do what it had to do. It was a classic situation of a military unit operating behind enemy lines but within a friendly population. The military unit depended heavily on that civilian population for a lot of the resources and personnel in order to do that job. And so they recognised as long as they could keep a handle on the civilian population within the enclave, that many of the men would not leave their families and as such would be available for military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you have information to the effect that the army, because it wanted to have its units at full strength, prevented the population from leaving Srebrenica in accordance with the agreement on free movement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen any specific ABiH documents that note that. However, I've -- as part of my own research, I've probably come across enough anecdotal information which would support that conclusion, which is that it was not in the interest of the ABiH government to allow the civilian population to slowly bleed out of the enclave, because of the impact that it would have on the military units within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Did you come across information that even the humanitarian aid was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Tolimir please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters asked you to repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, as you reviewed various material, did you come to learn that the army in Srebrenica and Zepa compelled the civilians to work for the purposes of the army in order to receive humanitarian aid -- in exchange of which work they would receive humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you're -- when you use the phrase "compelled the civilians to work for the purposes of the army," are you referring to -- I mean, just to be clear, are we referring to actual physical labour or are we referring to the idea that the men would have to serve in the military, at least part time, in order to be eligible for humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I don't need the answer merely for the sake of an answer. Perhaps we should look at a document -- or, rather, I will put another question to you and then we will have before us a document which deals with this issue. Here, on page 2, the last paragraph of this document, wasn't this problem in Zepa resolved by the application of restrictive measures and even by the deployment of units to Zepa which were to prevent the population from moving out? Let's look at the last paragraph on this page. Perhaps in your language it's not the last paragraph. "In addition to other measures, I decided to send to Zepa elements of a unit attached to the staff and the commander of the 281st Light Mountain Brigade, Major Zulfo Tursunovic, to use his authority to try and bring back some of the individuals who hailed from these areas who we believe left in the direction of Zepa in the last couple of nights with a view to crossing over to the Kladanj area. As appropriate, the members of this unit will, in co-operation with the military police of the 285th Light Mountain Brigade, arrest these individuals and return them to Srebrenica by force. "We believe that the 2nd Corps should, in co-operation with other authorities, take more severe repressive measures against all these individuals, which would be a deterrent to all those who wished to move out of Srebrenica and Zepa." This was signed by Major Ramiz Becirovic. This is my question: In the course of 1995, was it not the case that the problem had become so serious that the army had to prevent individuals from leaving the enclaves? They even had to resort to oppressive measures, and even the involvement of the corps was required to make sure that these people are prevented from fleeing the area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, as this document reflects, the military leadership of the 28th Division recognised the adverse impact that these desertions were having on its military units, much the same way that they impacted the military units of the VRS and other units. And along the same lines, they were engaged in measures to try and apprehend these individuals, even if they had successfully left the enclave, and then return them to their military units, in part, as is noted, as a deterrent. So that if these people who had thought they had successfully deserted were brought back, in the future other people would recognise that attempts to desert would be futile and that they should just stay and perform their military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, can we have your comments as a military expert and military analyst how this reflected itself on the humanitarian needs in the enclaves? Were they greater or smaller as a result of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question, because I'm not sure I understand how a correlation between military members deserting from the 28th Division -- I mean, I'm not sure how it connects to the overall humanitarian situation in Srebrenica. If you could clarify your question, maybe I can assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Was the number of beneficiaries of the humanitarian aid reduced with the departure of the people from the enclaves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, obviously every mouth that's no longer required to be fed makes it the same amount of supplies go further among the remaining population. If those families were to abandon their residence in Srebrenica, those facilities would then become available to other people who may not have had a place to stay or things of that nature. So, you know, arguably, as people departed the enclave, and if one assumes that the supply remained constant, those people remaining in the enclave could expect to enjoy a slightly higher quality of life, or at least a slight -- not quality of life, certainly a slightly increased ability for food and housing and other services.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were humanitarian organisations aware of this? Did they, due to these departures, reduce the amount of the humanitarian aid they delivered or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at D209, a document dating back to 1995, and let's make a comparison of it. Mr. Butler, look at the table relating to Srebrenica and the months of March and April. The figure for March is 305. And in April it had 387 tonnes. So it increased from 305 to 387 tonnes. And then flour, which is in the first row, also increased. So from -- in Gorazde, 362 to 531. Zepa, 72 -- from 72 to 77. So that's just the first row. In other words, regardless of the fact that the size of the population was reduced, the needs increased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question was this: If we look at the first row in this table, can we conclude that the quantities of humanitarian aid increased despite the fact that the population decreased?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that all you can conclude based on this document is that from the month of March and April that, with respect to looking at line 1 as an example, flour, that the amount increased between March and April. I don't believe that - based on this document and one or two others - that anybody can draw a meaningful conclusion as to why the amount increased and, more importantly, that it was directly as a result of a -- or that the population was decreasing at the same time, and by how much. I mean, just looking at the dates between March and April, right offhand one reason that I could possibly attribute to the increased delivery would be the fact that March still falls at the end of winter and April begins the month of spring when the weather is more temperate; that might have allowed for better conditions for convoys to move in. I don't know that that's the case, but it is another explanation. So the practice of taking one or two data points and trying to extrapolate a conclusion out of that in this regard is just not an exercise I'm going to engage in. There are ways to come to these conclusions through proper analysis, but this isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Did you yourself make any sort of an assessment or analysis of the shipments of humanitarian aid received on a monthly basis in the course of 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you've asked me that question before, and my answer again remains the same: It was beyond the scope of my analytical work to analyse UN supplies going into the convoys and -- or UNHCR supplies going into the enclaves. I did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But in the course of your examination-in-chief, you expressed views and positions about the humanitarian aid being on a steady decrease; whereas, we can see on the basis of this document that it was on the increase. So did you look into the validity of your answers from that perspective?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The testimony that I made with respect to the examination-in-chief was the result of, one, the fact that I was being -- I was reviewing documents which showed that the Main Staff was reviewing convoy orders and, for their reasons, were making reductions in the amount of material supplies that they were allowing UNPROFOR and the United Nations UNHCR organisation to bring into the enclaves. That was the point that I was trying to make. I did not correlate that to the point that you're looking at, is whether or not those actual reductions that was being made by the Main Staff in fact resulted in a net increase or decrease in the amount of supplies going into the Srebrenica enclave or the Zepa enclave. That analysis can be done. It wasn't within my purview to do it. Many of the documents that you're bringing up now were not available to me when I did my initial analysis. So, again, the purpose of my testimony in direct with respect to those convoy documents was to show the Court the involvement of the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska in that process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, please have a look on the screen again. Mr. Tolimir dealt with item 1, flour. If you have a short look at the other items, do you see an increase or a decrease or a stable amount of food being delivered in the months between March and April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, again, sir, as soon as you go to item 2, you see an increase. In item 3, looking at the Srebrenica column, you see a decrease. Item 4 remains stable. And this is the point that I'm trying to make: You can't make what's logically known as an ipso facto analytical conclusion, which is an analytical trap, I mean, you can't draw these types of conclusions just like this. I mean, if you're going to do a sustained analysis of what food was reaching the enclaves and what the conditions were, yes, you can do that, but this is why I cannot agree to General Tolimir's conclusion simply off of one or two data points and that they may or may not support a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, I don't see you any longer on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was -- I can't really make much sense of the B/C/S that's covering the English, and you and Mr. Butler are so, and so I'm not going to -- I won't worry about that. But if we were going to go into that any more, we're just asking if we can see the entire image. But we're fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I received the response I was asking for. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, some minutes left before the second break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, the staple foods -- aren't flour and beans such staple foods, and isn't that the sort of food stuff you would need to consume every day?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be a rough diet if it were just those two, but, yes, I take your point, flour and beans are staple items.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And what about powdered milk? Isn't that the criterion based on which one would assess the needs of a population for each of the month?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, without knowing more details as to the overall situation, within the enclave -- and I -- just at this point let's take Srebrenica, you know, without knowing the number of total people that they're trying to supply the existing food stocks and consumption rates, this is kind of the same discussion that we had a number of days ago when you asked me the question about whether or not, if I were to look at a list of ammunition, whether that was enough, and my same answer applies: Enough in context to what? Without knowing what is already on hand and how fast it's being consumed, there's no way to make any kind of informed assessment as to whether or not the supplies that are being received are enough. All you can do is exactly what you're doing here, which is pointing to two specific data points on a month-by-month basis and making a calculation that, you know, between the months of March and April one data point increased and one data point decreased. That tells you nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we must have our second break now. I would like to invite you to consider if you could leave to another -- move to another matter after the break, because Mr. Butler clearly indicated that he is not an expert on these matters you have put questions to him. We adjourn, and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, let us look at 65 ter document 05179. When I asked you yesterday, on page 16492, about document P162, you gave me more or less this answer, as recorded in the transcript. When I asked you about your position and your understanding about the role of the co-ordinating body mentioned here and its relationship with the Main Staff, you gave your answer in lines 2 to 19 on page 16492. You said that the UN was not the only agency involved in these matters. Now, in order to avoid repetition: At the end of your answer, I asked you about your opinion as to who had control about what was entering the enclave -- actually, that was the Prosecutor who asked you this, and you said that it was the Main Staff who issued specific approvals and permissions on a daily basis. Now, please, let us look now at 65 ter 05178.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and as the general appears to be asking Mr. Butler about a specific question that I did, and his specific answer, and he paraphrased it, could he -- could we actually go to that, if he intends to do that, so we can see what the question was and what the answer was? It's, I think, a rather important area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Up to now we didn't hear any question from Mr. Tolimir. He referred to a previous part of the examination --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When document P2162 was shown, on transcript page 16492, lines 12 to 19, the Prosecutor asked: "Can you explain how you understand the role of the co-ordinating body ...?" And I would like to read the answer that you gave, lines 2 to 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's a waste of time to read that into the transcript again. We have all the transcript in front of us in the English version. The witness can see it and read it again. Perhaps you put a question in relation to that, and then Mr. Butler is in the position to read the relevant part of his previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the second answer to Mr. McCloskey about who had the final control, you said that it was the Main Staff who issued definite -- definitive orders on a daily basis. Now, my question was: Did you have control in mind or approvals? Because Mr. McCloskey asked you about control and you spoke about approvals. So let us clarify to what your answer exactly refer. Which term should we use, whether it be "control" or "approval"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this is in relation to the lines 18, 19, 20, and 21 of page 16492.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I stand by my answer. My opinion is that on a factual basis ultimately the Main Staff exercised the final control, because the fact is that regardless of any decisions made by the civilian body, it would ultimately have to be the army that would permit the convoys to transit through what were then military areas to get into the enclaves. So while I take General Tolimir's point that ultimately the approval body was the civilian body, the reality on the ground was that the civilian body could approve requests as they saw fit; but ultimately if the Main Staff did not allow the convoy to transit through for a variety of military reasons, the Main Staff was exercising control over that process. I hope that clarifies, sir -- that clarifies the meaning behind my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I recall that you described that in more detail later on in your examination-in-chief, but could you make a distinction between the word "control," final control, which was used by Mr. McCloskey, and your answer "the final approval." Because now you said you stand by your answer but use the word "control" instead of "approval." Could you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess -- I guess to be very -- as clear as I can on it: Again, the civilian agency approves the request from UNHCR. That request then goes to the Main Staff. The Main Staff ultimately controls the access that that convoy is going to have to the enclave, because first it has to also review that material. It has the option of, as we saw in a number of documents, writing down some of the supplies that were going through and potentially sending them back to the civilian commission for them to reconsider that those degradations could take place. It is also responsible, if it approves or concurs with the approval of Republika Srpska civilian commission, ultimately it's the army that's responsible and for ensuring that clearance is delivered so the convoy can go into the territory of the Republika Srpska and be delivered. So the Main Staff and the military controls that aspect of the process which will ultimately result in delivery of the convoy and the goods to the enclave. But in the sense of the UN civilian goods, as we've discussed, again, I take General Tolimir's point that, you know, it is a civilian body that is that approval authority. I agree that, in theory, the civilians are going to approve it and the military is just going to follow orders and do that; however, for a variety of reasons the military may seek at points in times to delay those convoys, to reroute those convoys, things of that nature. So, I mean, there's a de jure process and then there's what actually happens on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, for that. Mr. Tolimir, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, was it possible for the army to prohibit a convoy to pass through if it had been given an approval to do so by the state committee?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that from the experience of the documents that I have seen that if the state committee wanted the convoy to go through, and if the military objected to it, that the military could come up with necessary pretexts which might delay that convoy or might, again, push it in time or maybe even deal with the issue of the -- how much cargo was in the convoy. But I would say that at the end of the day, if the civilians approved that convoy going through, the VRS - unless they could actually show sustained combat activity in an area - would ultimately have to accede to that and allow that convoy to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, let us look at 65 ter document 05178. It's a document from the Main Staff of the VRS, dated the 21st of March, 1995. It is addressed to the state committee for co-operation with the UN and international humanitarian organisations to the chairman of the committee, Professor Koljevic, personally. And the document reads as follows: "On the 20th of March, we received a letter from the chief of convoy operation of the UNPROFOR BH command, Lieutenant Leviv [phoen], who, in response to our letter regarding the reduction and rationalisation of the movement of convoys in order to ease the burden on our roads, sent the follow answer: 'That he appreciates the concern on the part of the VRS army concerning the safety of UNPROFOR personnel on the roads and accepts the proposal for the traffic to be reduced as much as possible by establishing fixed schedules for convoys.' "That is why they want to introduce a shuttle bus line for the main company of BH command in order to transport only those UNPROFOR personnel who are going on leave or are on rotation and travelling from Sarajevo to Split and vice versa. The cargo accompanying these convoys would only consist of personal belongings and mail pouches. Depending on the number of passengers, a convoy may be made up of one minibus or one jeep or a bigger bus or a combination thereof. I propose the following days where they would travel: "Tuesday, Sarajevo-Split. And then back on Wednesday. "Saturday, Sarajevo-Split. And then back on Sunday. "The request for these movements shall be submitted to the Main Staff of the VRS through regular procedure through military observers at Pale. "We are forwarding this to you for your information, and we are asking the state committee for co-operation with the UN to adopt a decision regarding the said requests, and we need to have it in writing. "Chief of Staff, Manojlo Milovanovic." I'm sorry for having to read this because we don't have a translation. My question is: Does this document suggest that Lieutenant General Manojlo Milovanovic is asking Professor Koljevic, the chairman of the committee, not to take any decision but, rather, just to implement it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I take this document to be is, first of all, a note from Lieutenant General Milovanovic that lays out the issue of UNPROFOR traffic and wanting to standardise it, that they have proposed a solution on how travel will be made in this particular case. And it sounds like, again, from the last two paragraphs, that General Milovanovic is forwarding this proposal up to the civilian leadership for them to ratify, and the presumption being, once the civilian leadership ratifies this formally in writing it will be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you noticed that this is not the only thing that he is forwarding but that in the last two paragraphs he is seeking a decision to be made on the said requests, and I am going to quote again the last two lines: "We are forwarding the above to you for your information, and we are kindly asking the state committee for co-operation with United Nations to take a decision on the said request, which needs to be sent to the Main Staff of the VRS in writing. "Chief of Staff, Lieutenant General Manojlo Milovanovic." So is he asking the state committee to make a decision or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Maybe I wasn't clear with what I said back or there was a translation issue, but I believe that is exactly what is happening. He is making this proposal to the state commission and he is requesting that they make a formal decision on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now look at P689, Article 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, are you tendering this last document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, we would like to tender this, and my apologies for not stating that right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 5178 shall be assigned Exhibit D308 marked for identification pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the second page of this Official Gazette in the Serbian version so that we can see what we are reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, could you please look at Article 6, which reads: "Permits for the movement of convoys and employees of the UN and humanitarian organisations on the territory of Republika Srpska shall be issued by the co-ordinating body for humanitarian operations, pursuant to committee decisions." My question is: Did General Milovanovic strictly abide to all rules and regulations in light of this decision that was published in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly is consistent with the language in Article 6, reflecting, in a practical sense, that the military is going to lay out the option in this particular case and send it up for a final decision by the civilian leadership. So taking the last exhibit in this one in context, General Milovanovic appears to be operating within the framework of the spirit of Article 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have P2162, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we are waiting, let me tell you that it's a document produced by the Main Staff entitled -- or, actually, sent to subordinate units of Drina Corps, Eastern Bosnia Corps, and Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The original says 2nd of April, 1995. With respect to this document, you commented this handwritten remark made by Mr. Nikolic, and I'm going to read it: "Not a single convoy or the ICRC team or MSF may enter Srebrenica without my permission and presence. "Signed, Momir Nikolic." Now, my question is: Did Momir Nikolic make this remark and address it to the Main Staff prior to the convoys entering Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that in the context of this document Momir Nikolic is making this remark to the Main Staff. I believe that my testimony related to this is that this document was sent by the Main Staff to the subordinate formations, to include the Drina Corps, and made its way to Captain First Class Nikolic of the Bratunac Brigade who was responsible for the inspection of those vehicles is going into the enclave. And that this notation on the document is for the benefit of the individuals at the yellow bridge and at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters so that they would know that in the event that one of these convoys were to come in and seek to enter the enclave, that they were not authorised to grant permission for that convoy to continue on unless Captain Nikolic was personally present there and gave his authorisation. I believe I've also testified that this is an example of the type of inspection regime that was in place so that the VRS had the ability to inspect these convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Can you please tell me this: Did Nikolic write this because he wanted to obey orders to the letter and exercising conduct control in a proper way, or was his intention to impose some kind of his personal authority?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Your first supposition is what I believe is the correct one. Captain Nikolic wrote these orders because he himself had received orders through the chain of command to ensure the proper inspection and clearance of these convoys at the last possible place that they could be inspected before they entered the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. The first sentence reads: "We hereby inform you that we agree to the requests of the co-ordinating body for humanitarian aid as follows." And then they are citing the requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would just note - and I know it's difficult for the interpreters to always read the translation, but it says "we --" the official translation says: "We hereby inform you that we consent ..." So "agree"/"consent" is the issue here. So I just wanted to point that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we please move to the last sentence of this document. Let's see what else General Milovanovic has to say. This is page 3 of the document, and the last. Can it be shown in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm reading: "Chef d'équipe," or head of team, "will be carrying the cargo manifests as well as the manifests of the individuals being transported, conduct inspection, and ensure a smooth passage." "Chief of Staff, Lieutenant General Manojlo Milovanovic." My question is: Does this part of the document speak of any restrictions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. The English page doesn't correspond to the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told that only the first page of the English version is uploaded into e-court so that that part is not available in English. But you read it into the transcript and you may put, now, your question to Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, did General Milovanovic ask that inspection be strictly carried out as well as that the convoy be allowed unhindered passage?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a two-part process. Yes, he directed that the inspections be carried out; and by noting the fact that, one, he transmitted down what the Main Staff's understanding of the cargo was going to be, and he also indicated that the convoy commander is going to be carrying a copy of the manifest, this way Captain [sic] Milovanovic had a way of not only making sure that the cargo in the vehicle matched the cargo that the convoy commander had on the manifest, but that that cargo also matched what the Main Staff understood was being set down. If all of those conditions are met, then the second prong of that goes into effect, which is: Yes, ones these conditions are satisfied, the expectation is that Captain Momir Nikolic will allow the convoy to pass unhindered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question for you: Was Captain Nikolic able to deny passage to a convoy that had been granted approval by General Milovanovic, a convoy which had a complete cargo manifest?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the cargo manifests matched, then Captain Nikolic would not, if he were properly exercising his authority, be able to stop the convoy on that basis. If the cargo manifests did not match or there were some other problem that was identified, I suspect the practical application would be that Captain Nikolic would contact, through the Drina Corps, the Main Staff, he would explain what the discrepancies were as they existed, and he would request instructions from the Main Staff as to what to do with the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Since we are running out of time, let us move to a video-clip concerning the ammunition found on a humanitarian convoy at Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which is P212. The transcript is 1D234. And it has been distributed to the interpreters. Can it be played, please. P2126. I omitted number 6. Can it be played, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Representatives of the UNHCR transported --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can we note, the interpreters: We have received a transcript, but we don't know where the tape is being played for and cannot read the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should stop the video. The interpreters indicated they don't know where the tape is being played for and cannot read the transcript. Can that be checked by the Defence, please. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am told by the Case Manager that the transcripts of the video "UNHCR Convoy - Rogatica (Zepa)" were distributed to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interprets note that the portion heard on the footage so far is not reflected in the transcript that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The video fully reflects the transcript, and nothing has been left out or added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, I would like to receive the transcript in hard copy to be able to check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have copies ready and are able to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The only way to resolve this problem is that the video should start exactly where the transcript is beginning. And it should be noted for our transcript, for the record, where the video will start. One moment, please. Don't start. Mr. Gajic, could you please check with your colleague that we really start with where the words can be heard: "Along with food for the people of the Muslim enclave of Zepa ..." And please indicate, for the record, where we start with the video. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm afraid that we will have to start from the beginning because the Case Manager doesn't have the headphones. And the video starts, of course, from 00.00, and we will play the entire video footage. It is short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please, and the interpreters will only be able to interpret that portions we have -- they have available.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Along with food for the people of the Muslim enclave of Zepa, the UNHCR representatives were transporting ammunition for Muslim soldiers. "At the Rogatica check-point, a routine inspection of the convoy loaded at the UNHCR -- loaded at the UNHCR warehouse in Pancevo, turned up ammunition of various calibres hidden among the goods, mainly in the flour, and in the cabs of the trucks. "VRS soldier: While inspecting the convoy, in about the fifth sack I checked using a knife, I noticed there was something in the flour. When I carried out a regular inspection, I discovered ammunition. "Without a doubt this sort of conduct represents the severest form of criminal activity and is utterly in contradiction with the mandate and nature of humanitarian missions. "Whether or not they felt caught in the act by the ammunition found in the convoy, the leader and one of the drivers reacted as follows: "Convoy member: I don't know anything about the ammunition found in the flour, and I have nothing to say. "Convoy member: I don't know where the ammunition in the truck came from; I don't know what to say. I cannot say anything really. "Commander of the Army of Republika Srpska, Colonel General Ratko Mladic, sent protests to the UNHCR offices in Zagreb, Belgrade, and Pale, and asked that competent officials there take immediate measures to avoid similar incidents in the future. "General Mladic also informed the UNHCR representatives about the fate of the convoy that was stopped and its personnel. General Mladic's statement said that the goods will be confiscated and appropriate legal measures taken against those responsible. "What else can we say as we watch the images from Rogatica that best testify to the human nature of international humanitarian organisations? "Need we remind them that they have always been welcome and safe on the Serbian side in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina? "Need we remind them that the food for the Muslim population arrives in these convoys above all because of the understanding of the Serbs? "Need we remind them how many times this understanding has been abused? "Should they ask themselves who has the right to transport ammunition and weapons along with food?"
